newsitem.title: GERMANY: ALPINE SKIING-SEIZINGER SHOWS DISTINCTION ON SLOPES.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SEIZINGER SHOWS DISTINCTION ON SLOPES.

text.p: Purely because of her voice, Germany's Katja Seizinger stood out on the Alpine skiing circuit before she even won a race of any note .
Among the thick mountain accents of most of the skiers, Seizinger's neutral German tones are as distinctive as a dinner jacket on a building site.

Unlike many of her rivals, the defending overall World Cup champion was not born in the shadow of a mountain but in Germany's industrial Ruhr region where the highest point that snow normally reaches is the top of a chimney or a slag heap.
But Seizinger is more at home on racing pistes than many of the skiers who were born within a few metres of a ski lift. An Olympic downhill gold medal, world and World Cup victories vouch for that.

The world championships in Sestriere, however, provide a new challenge for the 24-year-old racer who is at her best in the speed disciplines but also proved in World Cup races in this German resort in January that she can challenge in giant slaloms and slaloms too.

Last year's championships in Sierra Nevada were largely a disappointment for the German team and for Seizinger who finished second in the downhill but was unable to make an impact in the super-G and the combined event.
The German's main goal this season is to win a medal at the world championships. Her last and only world title was in the super-G at the 1993 championships in Japan.
"I have won everything already but I think it would be fun to do it all again," she said. "Although ski racing is my job, it is also my passion."
Seizinger is, without doubt, one of Germany's most successful racers ever.
But the fact that she rarely shows emotion in public has led some journalists to label her arrogant and aloof. Those who know her well privately dispute this.
Former double Olympic champion Rosi Mittermaier, Germany's most famous female skier before Seizinger came along, is in no doubt about her skills, however.
"She is rare among the racers in so far as she has total
feeling for the ski," she said. "You can't learn that."

Seizinger's father Hans, a successful steel manufacturer, moved the family away from the Ruhr at the end of the 1970s. When she showed a flair for skiing, Seizinger went to a school closer to the mountains.
It turned out to be an inspired move.
